'''Aldemaro Romero Jr.''' (born September 11, 1951)<ref name="SiueAromero">{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/~aromero/|title=Aldemaro Romero (Jr.)|publisher=siue.edu|date=11 February 2013|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> is a [[Venezuela|Venezuelan/America]]n scientist, communicator, and public intellectual. He has published more than 1,100 works,<ref name="SiueDean">{{cite web|url=http://aromerojr.net/wordpress/publications/|title=Aldemaro Romero: Complete List of Publications|work=Aldemaro Romero Jr. |publisher=aromerojr.net|access-date=26 December 2018}}</ref> more than 30 books and monographs, and produced, directed, written and/or hosted more than 1500 radio shows and 400 TV shows and documentaries in areas ranging from science to history and philosophy.<ref name="CV">{{Cite web|url = https://www.aromerojr.net/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/CURRICULUM-VITAE-copy.Full_.pdf|title=CV|access-date=26 December 2018}}</ref> He is known for his approaches of combining field, laboratory and archival studies from different disciplines.

Romero served as dean  of the [[College of Arts and Sciences]] at [[Southern Illinois University Edwardsville]] until 2015 and became dean of the George and Mildred Weissman School of Arts and Sciences at [[Baruch College]]/[[City University of New York]], in July 2016.<ref>See Baruch College press release - http://www.baruch.cuny.edu/DrRomeroWeissmanDean.htm</ref> He was named Dean Emeritus by the International Council of Fine Arts Deans in 2021.<ref name="icfad">{{cite web|url=https://www.icfad.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=429:romera-al--bio&catid=31:bios-2019|access-date=4 July 2024 |title=Romera al, bio }}</ref> Also that year he became a visiting scholar at the University of Miami, FL.<ref name="linkedin">{{cite web|url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/aldemaro-romero-jr-49369a2b/|title=Aldemaro Romero Jr.|access-date=4 July 2024}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
[[File:Aldemaro Romero Jr. conducting his father's orchestra.tiff|thumb|Romero Jr. conducting his father's orchestra]]
Romero Jr. was born in [[Caracas]], Venezuela, the son of Venezuelan composer, pianist, and orchestra conductor [[Aldemaro Romero|Aldemaro Romero Sr.]] and his wife, Margot Díaz Saavedra de Romero. While listening to one of his father's records at home when he was four-years-old, his father saw him mimicking a conductor's mannerisms and had him appear on a live TV show conducting his orchestra. That and other TV appearances made him a celebrity in Venezuela even performing in movies conducting an orchestra.<ref name="Vimeo57406806">{{cite web|url=http://vimeo.com/57406806|title=Aldemaro Romero, Jr. Conducts on Vimeo|date=14 January 2013|publisher=vimeo.com|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> In adult life Romero never pursued a professional career as a musician but continued performing as an amateur.<ref name="Vimeo39887881">{{cite web|url=http://vimeo.com/39887881|title=Choral Society performance|date=6 April 2012|publisher=vimeo.com|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref><ref name="Vimeo59525356">{{cite web|url=http://vimeo.com/59525356|title=Carpe Diem String Quartet & Peter Soave: The Music of Aldemaro Romero on Vimeo|date=12 February 2013|publisher=vimeo.com|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref>

Romero attributes his decision to become a scientist the day the press announced the launch of [[Sputnik]]. His decision to study biology was inspired by the [[Jacques-Yves Cousteau]] film ''[[The Silent World]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.aromerojr.net/Publications/Romero.pdf|title = Romero's Curiosity Rooted in Undersea World|date = |access-date = |website = |publisher = }}</ref>

He obtained a [[Licenciatura]] in [[biology]], with a [[zoology]] concentration, from the [[Universitat de Barcelona]],<ref name="EduEn">{{cite web|url=https://www.ub.edu/web/ub/en/|title=Universitat de Barcelona|publisher=ub.edu|date=27 March 2013|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> in 1977, while working as a scientist in several institutions and as science writer for several printed, radio, and TV media. He obtained his doctorate in biology from the [[University of Miami]],<ref name="Miami">{{cite web|url=http://www.miami.edu/|title=University of Miami|publisher=miami.edu|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> in [[Coral Gables, Florida]], with a [[doctoral dissertation]] on the evolution and behavior of [[cavefish]].

==Career==
In 1994, he fled his native Venezuela to the United States, after denouncing the killing of dolphins by Venezuelan fishermen and receiving death threats. He paid a fisherman to dissect a live dolphin while he filmed the scene. He has taught at the [[University of Miami]], [[Miami Dade College|Miami-Dade Community College]], [[Florida Atlantic University]], [[Macalester College]], and [[Arkansas State University]]. Romero accepted the position as dean of the [[College of Arts and Sciences]] at [[Southern Illinois University Edwardsville]] in 2009, a position that he held until 2014. He became dean of the George and Mildred Weissman School of Arts and Sciences at [[Baruch College]]/[[City University of New York]], effective July 2016,<ref>See Baruch College press release: http://www.baruch.cuny.edu/DrRomeroWeissmanDean.htm</ref> and stepped down in June 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.icfad.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=269:bio-aldemaro-romero-jr-&catid=27:bios-2017|title = Bio Aldemaro Romero Jr}}</ref>

[[File:Aldemaro Romero Jr. At the Museum of Zoology of Barcelona.jpeg|thumb|Romero Jr. at the Museum of Zoology of Barcelona]]
As an undergraduate student in biology at the [[University of Barcelona|Universitat de Barcelona]] in Spain, Romero volunteered at the Museum of Zoology (later renamed as Museum of Natural Sciences) where he created the [[Hydrobiology]] Section <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Romero |first1=Aldemaro |title=La nueva Sección de Hidrobiología del Museo de Zoología de Barcelona. |journal=Miscelánea Zoologica |date=1972 |volume=3 |issue=2 |page=111 |url=http://www.aromerojr.net/Publications/002.NuevaSeccion%20deHidrobiologia.pdf |access-date=16 April 2021}}</ref> led a group of other undergraduates to work on aquatic organisms reorganizing some of the collections and re-identifying some of the mislabeled specimens. He also volunteered working at the Museum of Geology of the Seminario Conciliar of Barcelona where he described several new species of [[Middle Triassic]] (240-235&nbsp;million years old) [[horseshoe crab]]s and a set of fossils that he described as an entirely new group (subphylum) of animals never reported to science before.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Romero |first1=Aldemaro |title=Contributions in Paleontology and Evolutionary Biology. |date=2021 |publisher=Amazon Books |location=Seattle, WA |isbn=9798595546379 |pages=vi + 224 |edition=1st. |url=https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08Y49YYMX/ref=ox_sc_act_image_1?smid=A1Y53T3O3Q25L8&psc=1 |access-date=16 April 2021}}</ref>

===Cave biology===
[[File:Aldemaro Romero Jr. (center) with a group of collaborators at Cumaca Cave, Trinidad, W.I.jpg|thumb|Romero Jr. (center) with a group of collaborators at Cumaca Cave in [[Trinidad]]]]
As a graduate student at the University of Miami, Romero specialized on the study of the evolution, behavior, and ecology of [[cavefishes]]. Through these studies he was the first to propose that colonization of cave environments was an active process via behavioral adaptations preceding [[morphology (biology)|morphological]] ones (e.g. blindness and depigmentation).<ref name="Dissertation">{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/181.Astyanax_Fasciatus.Dissertation.pdf|title=Responses to light in cave and surface populations of Astyanax Fasciatus (Pisces: Characidae): an evolutionary interpretation|year=1984|author =Aldemaro Romero|publisher=University of Miami|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> Later he proposed a new hypothesis aimed at explaining the mechanisms leading towards the loss of eyes and pigmentation among these and other cave animals. He suggested that the mechanism behind this phenomenon was a little understood biological process at the time called [[phenotypic plasticity]]. This challenged the typological view of all cave creatures as completely differentiated from a genetic viewpoint from their surface (epigean) ancestors. According to Romero all what was needed for the evolution of drastically morphologically distinct cave species were just a few changes in the [[genes]] controlling the development of features such as eyes and pigmentation. These and other ideas were summarized in a book.<ref name="PDF543330641">{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/556.CaveBiology.pdf|date=4 February 2009|title=Cave Biology|author =Aldemaro Romero|publisher=Cambridge University Press|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref>

===Marine mammalogy===
[[File:Aldemaro Romero Jr. (left) teaching marine mammalogy at Arkansas State University dissecting a sea otter.jpg|thumb|Romero Jr. (left) dissecting a sea otter while teaching marine mammalogy at [[Arkansas State University]]]]
Romero studied the history and practices of exploitation of [[marine mammal]]s in the [[Caribbean basin]]. To that end he conducted field and archival studies in [[Venezuela]],<ref name="Venezuela">{{cite journal|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/326.ExploitationCetaceansVenezuela.pdf|journal=Rep. Int. Whal. Comm.|year=1997|volume=47|pages=735–746|title=Exploitation of Cetaceans in Venezuela|author1=Aldemaro Romero |author2=A. Ignacio Agudo |author3=Steven M. Green |access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> [[Trinidad and Tobago]],<ref name="MarMammTrinidad">{{cite journal|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/406.EnvironHistMarMammTrinidad.pdf|title=Environmental History of Marine Mammal Exploitation in Trinidad and Tobago, W.I., and its Ecological Impact|author1=Aldemaro Romero |author2=Ruth Baker |author3=Joel E. Creswell |author4=Anuradha Singh |author5=Annabelle Mckie |author6=Michael Manna |date=24 July 2002|journal=Environment and History|volume=8|pages=255–274|access-date=30 March 2013|doi=10.3197/096734002129342666|issue=3 |bibcode=2002EnHis...8..255R }}</ref> [[Grenada]],<ref name="Grenada">{{cite journal|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/363.PastPresentUrilizationMarineMammalsGrenada.pdf|journal=J. Cetacean Res. Manage|volume=2|issue=3|pages=223–226|year=2000|title=Past and present utilisation of marine mammals in Grenada, West Indies|author1=Aldemaro Romero |author2=Kyla Hayford |access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> [[Saint Vincent and the Grenadines|St Vincent and the Grenadines]], [[Barbados]], and [[Bermuda]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/497.Bermuda16Century.pdf|title=More Private Gain than Good: Whale and Ambergris Exploitation in 17th-Century Bermuda|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/546.WhalBerm18.pdf|title=Between War and Poverty: Whaling in 18th-Century Bermuda|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/562.WhalingBarbadosFinal.pdf|title=Chasing Fool's Gold: Whaling in 19th and 20th Century Bermuda|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> as well as in libraries and archives in the northeastern U.S. that keep logbooks from whaling vessels. He concluded that local shore whaling combined with [[Yankee whaling]] were responsible for the depletion of many whale and dolphin populations throughout the Caribbean basin and that both types of whaling influenced each other from a cultural viewpoint.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/672.Yankee_whaling_in_the_caribbean_basin_its_impact_in_a_historical_context.pdf|title=Yankee Whaling in the Caribbean Basin: Its Impact in a Historical Context|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> For example, he recorded chants by local Caribbean whalers that mimicked those of Yankee whalers from the nineteenth century, demonstrating that cultural influence.<ref name="YouTubeWhaler">{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pr-RyJ3W0Eg|title=Bequia whaler chanting Yankee whaling inspired songs|date=12 February 2013 |publisher=YouTube|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref>

===Paleontology===
[[File:Fossil of one of the paleocyphonautes described by Romero.jpg|thumb|Fossil of one of the paleocyphonautes described by Romero]]
Romero has described a number of fossil species of horseshoe crabs,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.academia.edu/2971033|format=PDF|title=Tarracolimulus rieki, nov. gen., nov. sp., nuevo limúlido del Triásico de Montreal - Alcover (Tarragona).|work=Cuadernos de Geología Ibérica 4:239-246. |date=January 1977 |publisher=Academia.edu|access-date=24 February 2015 |last1=Jr |first1=Aldemaro Romero }}</ref>  [[jellyfish]]es<ref name="CnidariansAlcover">{{cite journal|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/577.CnidariansAlcover.pdf|title=Medusoid Cnidarians from the Montral-Alcover Lagerstätten (Triassic), Northeastern Spain|author1=Aldemaro Romero |author2=Raymond R. Rogers |author3=Lisa A. Gershwin |journal=Batalleria: Revista de Paleontología|date=18 April 2011|issn=0214-7831|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> (of which there are very few good-quality fossil impressions from around the world) and a group of very unusual species that he grouped under the name of Paleocyphonates, which he described as a new [[subphylum]]. He proposed the hypothesis that these extinct, medium-size fossil impressions represented the adult stage of today existing larva [[cyphonautes]] and supported such hypothesis not only with paleontological information but with physiological and developmental biology data as well.<ref name="academia">{{cite web|url=https://www.academia.edu/2971449|title=On the evolutionary significance of the Paleocyphonautidae: how fossils and larvae impact evolutionary reconstructions. &#124; Aldemaro Romero Jr.|work=Batalleria 12:149-154. |date=January 2005 |publisher=academia.edu|access-date=2 February 2014 |last1=Jr |first1=Aldemaro Romero }}</ref>

===Environmental studies===
In addition to his studies on marine mammal exploitation in the [[Caribbean]], Romero also carried out a number of field and archival studies about the exploitation of other marine animals in the same region. One of those allowed him to discover that the first animal population depleted by Europeans in the American continent was of a [[pearl oyster]] species (''Pinctada imbricata'') off the coast of Venezuela. In 1996 he studied historical records and used information about the biology of these and other species to explain its rapid disappearance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/425.DeathandTaxes.pdf|title=Death and Taxes|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> Romero also conducted studies on the pollution caused by [[lead]] in [[gasoline]] in Venezuela – the only country in the Western Hemisphere that still produced [[Tetraethyllead|leaded gasoline]] at that time. Those studies showed high levels of that contaminant in the Venezuelan environment and leaded gasoline was later eliminated from the market.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/313.PlomoElEnemigoInvisible.pdf|title=Plomo: El Enemigo Invisible|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/322.EnvironmentalImpactLeadedGas.pdf|title=The Environmental Impact of Leaded Gasoline in Venezuela|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/565.theinvisibleenemy.pdf|title=The Invisible Enemy|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> He also produced a study about all of the environmental-related programs in U.S. higher education institutions. He concluded that the number of those programs always spiked after the electoral wins by Democratic presidents.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/460.NotAllAreCreatedEqual_1_.2005..pdf |title=Not All Are Created Equal: An Analysis of the EnvironmentalPrograms/Departments in U.S. Academic Institutions From 1900 Until May 2005|access-date=27 August 2015 |url-status = dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023052539/http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/460.NotAllAreCreatedEqual_1_.2005..pdf |archive-date=23 October 2013 }}</ref>

===History and philosophy of science===
[[File:Aldemaro Romero Jr. at the entrance of Charles Darwin's home, Down House.jpg|thumb|Romero Jr. at the entrance of Charles Darwin's home, Down House]]
Romero has published and taught on the [[history and philosophy of science]], particularly on evolutionary ideas. Through his work he concluded that the initial resistance by French biologists to accept [[Charles Darwin]]'s ideas was a combination of catholic [[mysticism]] and nationalism.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/487.Oxford.pdf|title=The big issue between science and religion: purpose vs. uncertainty|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> In another study he concluded that environmental classification and intellectual inertia delayed for centuries the acceptance of [[whales and dolphins]] as mammals, instead of being considered fish.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/671.When_whales_became_mammals_the_scientific_journey_of_cetaceans_from_fish_to_mammals_in_the_history_of_science.pdf|title=When Whales Became Mammals: The Scientific Journey of Cetaceans From Fish to Mammals in the History of Science|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref> He has also worked on Darwin's life and published an analysis on how the British scientist was modifying his home at [[Downe]], [[Kent]], in order to accommodate to his scientific interests, his growing family and number of servants, as well as his health problems. To that end he developed an interactive house plan that shows the modifications he made through time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/675.Darwin_s_bubble.pdf|title=CHARLES DARWIN'S BUBBLE: THE EVOLUTION OF DOWN HOUSE |publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref>

===Science communication and public outreach===
Romero has promoted [[public awareness of science|public understanding of science]] and the liberal arts, from hosting radio and TV shows, to producing documentaries. He has contributed to the Spanish newspaper El Noticiero Universal, [[Radio Nacional de España]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rtve.es/radio/ |title=Radio Nacional de España |publisher=RTVE.es |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> [[Televisión Española]], {{Interlanguage link|Radio Peninsular|es|vertical-align=sup}}, [[Radio Capital]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eluniversal.com/aniversario/100/100a_art_radio-capital_23A2409643.shtml |title=100a_art_radio Capital_23A2409643 - Aniversario |language=es |publisher=El Universal |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> [[Venevision]], the Jonesboro Sun<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.jonesborosun.com |title=jonesborosun.com |publisher=jonesborosun.com |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> and the [[Edwardsville Intelligencer]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theintelligencer.com |title=The Edwardsville Intelligencer: Hometown News You Can't Miss! |publisher=Theintelligencer.com |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/CT_CollegeTalk.html |title=CAS - College Talk |publisher=Siue.edu |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> among others. He also hosted his own radio shows on [[KASU]], the college radio station at [[Arkansas State University]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kasu.org |title=Unique and Enriching, Member Supported Radio |publisher=KASU |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> and [[WSIE]] at SIU, Edwardsville.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wsie.com |title=WSIE 88.7 |publisher=WSIE |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/CASsegue.html |title=CAS - Segue Radio Show |publisher=Siue.edu |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> His work has also appeared in several scholarly publications.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/pdf/deanspublications/561.Communicating_Science.pdf|title=Communicating Science: New Agendas in Communication|publisher=Siue.edu|access-date=24 February 2015}}</ref>

===Non-profit and university administrator===
Romero served as a [[program director]] for [[The Nature Conservancy]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.org |title=Nature Conservancy &#124; Protecting Nature, Preserving Life |publisher=Nature.org |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=October 2020}} in Washington, DC, then as founder and executive director of BIOMA, The Venezuelan Foundation for the Conservation of Biological Diversity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://docs.google.com/file/d/0B79aV7DSzbwSNTZYM05aR0VlTkk/edit |title=BIOMA.pdf - Google Drive |work=Google Docs |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> He has also served as the director of the [[environmental studies]] program at [[Macalester College]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.macalester.edu |title=Macalester College: Private Liberal Arts College |publisher=Macalester.edu |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> chair of the biological sciences department at [[Arkansas State University]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.astate.edu |title=A-State |publisher=Astate.edu |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> and dean of the [[College of Arts and Sciences]] at [[Southern Illinois University Edwardsville]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siue.edu/artsandsciences/ |title=College of Arts & Sciences |publisher=Siue.edu |access-date=19 August 2013}}</ref> He became dean of the George and Mildred School of Arts and Sciences at [[Baruch College]]/[[City University of New York]], effective July 2016.<ref>See Baruch College press release http://www.baruch.cuny.edu/DrRomeroWeissmanDean.htm</ref> His approach to higher education emphasizes [[experiential learning]]. He has also been an advocate for the value of a [[liberal arts education]] and has produced instructional videos and spoken in public and professional forums.<ref name="YoutubeWatch">{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BKercxj0cCI|title=Aldemaro Romero Jr - The Importance of the Humanities and Social Sciences in Local Communities|date=9 November 2012 |publisher=YouTube|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref> He has led a number of initiatives to develop academic and cultural exchanges between the U.S. and [[Cuba]], exemplified by the agreement between [[Southern Illinois University, Edwardsville]] and the [[University of Havana]] and other Cuban cultural institutions.<ref name="Vimeo55283338">{{cite web|url=http://vimeo.com/55283338|title=Academic Diplomacy: An Expedition to Cuba|publisher=Vimeo|date=September 2012|access-date=30 March 2013}}</ref>

===Artistic productions===
Romero has been involved with the visual and performing arts organizing flashmobs, day-long art festivals or Art-a-Thons, while conducting his father's music to critical acclaim.<ref name="wordpress">{{cite web|url=https://newyorkmusicdaily.wordpress.com/2017/11/19/romeros/|title=Celebrating an Eclectic, Dynamic Force in Venezuelan Classical Music|website=New York Music Daily|date=19 November 2017 |access-date=19 March 2019}}</ref> He and his wife are collectors and patrons of visual arts. Pieces of their collections have been exhibited in New York City galleries.<ref name="cuny">{{cite web|url=http://www.baruch.cuny.edu/MishkinGallerySelfTaughtArtRomero.htm|website=baruch.cuny.edu|title=Mishkin Gallery Self-Taught Art – Romero Collection|access-date=19 March 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Romero met his wife Ana during the early 1970s while both were undergraduate students at the Universitat de Barcelona.{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}}
